pharm: A recombinant form of human erythropoietin that stimulates red-blood-cell production, used to treat anaemia of chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy-associated anaemia
quick: CKD: initial ~20 IU/kg SC three times weekly (or 40 IU/kg IV), titrate to target Hb; chemotherapy anaemia per SmPC
Use only if clearly needed; monitor blood pressure/Hb
Caution; limited data, likely minimal milk transfer of large protein
Used in renal anaemia; titrate to Hb, do not exceed target
Haemoglobin, blood pressure, iron studies, potassium; thrombosis signs
summary: Recombinant human erythropoietin beta (epoetin beta) is an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent that reproduces the action of endogenous erythropoietin, stimulating proliferation and differentiation of erythroid precursors to increase red-cell mass. It is used to treat symptomatic anaemia of chronic kidney disease, chemotherapy-induced anaemia in patients with non-myeloid malignancy, and to increase autologous blood yield, with dosing individualised and titrated to a target haemoglobin. Epoetin beta is licensed in the EU (e.g. as NeoRecormon) rather than by the FDA, so this monograph is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF sources. As a class, ESAs carry serious risks: targeting higher haemoglobin (above about 11-12 g/dL) increases cardiovascular, thrombotic and mortality risk, and in some cancer settings ESAs have shortened survival/time to tumour progression; they can also raise blood pressure and, rarely, cause pure red-cell aplasia from anti-erythropoietin antibodies. Iron status must be adequate for response.
indications: Symptomatic anaemia associated with chronic kidney disease (dialysis and non-dialysis patients)
Symptomatic chemotherapy-induced anaemia in patients with non-myeloid malignancy
Increasing the yield of autologous blood in predonation programmes
Prevention/treatment of anaemia of prematurity (per SmPC)

dosage.d: Subcutaneous: about 20 IU/kg three times weekly initially (may increase stepwise); intravenous: about 40 IU/kg three times weekly initially
dosage.t: SC or IV, three times weekly; titrate at intervals of about 4 weeks
dosage.n: Aim for a controlled Hb rise (not more than ~2 g/dL/month); do not exceed target Hb

dosage.d: Reduce to the lowest dose that maintains Hb in the target range (commonly ~10-12 g/dL)
dosage.t: SC or IV; frequency reduced as tolerated
dosage.n: Use the lowest dose to avoid the need for transfusion

dosage.d: Commonly 30000 IU per week (or weight-based per SmPC), adjusted by Hb response
dosage.n: Discontinue ~4 weeks after end of chemotherapy; ensure adequate iron

dosage.d: Per SmPC, given over the predonation period with iron supplementation
dosage.n: Reserve for patients with moderate anaemia and no iron deficiency

admin: Administer subcutaneously or intravenously as indicated; do not shake the solution
Ensure adequate iron stores (and correct folate/B12 deficiency) before and during therapy - response fails without sufficient iron
Control blood pressure before and during treatment; titrate dose slowly to avoid rapid haemoglobin rise
Use the lowest dose that reduces the need for transfusion; do not target normal/high haemoglobin
Investigate sudden loss of response for pure red-cell aplasia or other causes; do not switch ESAs if antibody-mediated PRCA is suspected
moa: Epoetin beta is a glycoprotein produced by recombinant DNA technology that is biologically indistinguishable in action from endogenous erythropoietin. It binds the erythropoietin receptor on erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow, stimulating their proliferation, differentiation and survival and the release of reticulocytes into the circulation, thereby increasing red-cell mass and haemoglobin. Endogenous erythropoietin is normally produced by the kidney in response to hypoxia; in chronic kidney disease this production is deficient, which the recombinant hormone replaces. The erythropoietic response requires adequate iron and other haematinics.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to epoetins or excipients
Pure red-cell aplasia following previous treatment with any erythropoietin
relative: Recent myocardial infarction or stroke; significant cardiovascular/thrombotic history
Untreated iron, folate or vitamin B12 deficiency
Active malignancy where ESA risk-benefit is unfavourable (potential to shorten survival)
Patients in whom anticoagulation prophylaxis is contraindicated (autologous predonation use)
monitor: Haemoglobin (to avoid exceeding target and rapid rise)
Serum potassium and signs of thrombosis
Response to therapy (investigate loss of response)

preg: There are limited data on epoetin beta in pregnancy. It should be used during pregnancy only when the expected benefit outweighs the potential risk, with careful monitoring of blood pressure and haemoglobin.
lact: It is not known whether epoetin beta passes into breast milk in clinically relevant amounts; as a large glycoprotein, oral absorption by the infant is likely minimal. Use with caution and weigh benefit against risk.
renal: Epoetin beta is a mainstay of treatment for anaemia of chronic kidney disease. Dose is titrated to haemoglobin response rather than reduced for renal function; avoid exceeding the target haemoglobin and control blood pressure and potassium.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is defined for hepatic impairment.

moderate: Iron status - response is blunted by iron deficiency; supplement iron as needed
Concomitant prothrombotic states/drugs - additive thrombosis risk
minor: May increase requirement for heparin during haemodialysis as haematocrit rises
interactions.diagnostics: Raises haemoglobin/haematocrit and reticulocytes; may increase serum potassium; monitor iron indices and blood pressure

common: Hypertension or worsening of existing hypertension
serious: Thromboembolic events (DVT, pulmonary embolism, stroke, MI)
Pure red-cell aplasia due to anti-erythropoietin antibodies
Increased mortality/tumour progression when targeting high Hb, especially in cancer
rare: Severe cutaneous reactions (SJS/TEN reported with ESAs)

monitoring: Haemoglobin frequently during initiation and dose changes, then regularly (avoid exceeding target and rapid rises)
Iron indices (ferritin, transferrin saturation) and other haematinics
Signs/symptoms of thrombosis; investigate any sudden loss of efficacy for pure red-cell aplasia
counsel: This injection helps your body make more red blood cells to treat anaemia
Keep your blood-pressure and blood-test appointments; very high blood counts can be dangerous
Report severe headaches, visual changes, chest pain, breathlessness, leg swelling or weakness/numbness, which may signal high blood pressure or a clot
Take any iron supplements as advised, since the treatment will not work well without enough iron
Do not aim for a higher blood count than your doctor recommends; the lowest effective dose is safest
pk: Reticulocyte rise within days; clinically meaningful haemoglobin increase over 2-6 weeks
Subcutaneous serum concentrations peak roughly 12-28 hours after injection
Approximately 4-12 hours after IV; effective half-life longer after subcutaneous dosing
Erythropoietic effect persists with regular dosing; lowest effective dose maintained
Store refrigerated (2-8 C); do not freeze; protect from light; do not shake
pearls: NOTE: Epoetin beta is an EU-licensed (EMA/SmPC, e.g. NeoRecormon) product and is NOT separately FDA-approved; this monograph is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF sources
ESA class risks: targeting high haemoglobin (>~11-12 g/dL) increases cardiovascular, thrombotic and mortality risk; in cancer it may shorten survival/time to progression
Use the LOWEST dose that avoids transfusion and do not exceed the target haemoglobin; avoid Hb rise >2 g/dL per month
Iron deficiency is the commonest cause of poor response - ensure adequate iron stores
Sudden loss of response with falling reticulocytes suggests antibody-mediated pure red-cell aplasia - stop and do not switch ESAs
Control blood pressure before and during treatment; monitor potassium in CKD
missed: If a dose is missed, contact your healthcare provider for advice on rescheduling; do not give two doses close together to make up. Maintaining a steady schedule keeps the blood count stable.
overdose: Excessive dosing can cause an excessive rise in haemoglobin/haematocrit with increased risk of hypertension, thrombosis and, in extreme cases, polycythaemia requiring phlebotomy. There is no specific antidote; withhold therapy, manage blood pressure and thrombotic complications, and perform venesection if polycythaemia is severe.
